newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RUGBY UNION-NZ'S LAST RUGBY "HARD MAN" RETIRES.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-NZ'S LAST RUGBY "HARD MAN" RETIRES.

text.p: Richard Loe, the last "hard man" of New Zealand rugby union, retired on Thursday.

The former All Black prop has been forced out of the game by a serious neck injury sustained in the Waikato Chiefs' last Super 12 match of the season, the New Zealand Rugby Football Union (NZRFU) said.
An All Black from 1986 to 1995, Loe's first-class career spanneed 20 years. But he will be remembered above all for his aggressive style of rugby.

Loe was suspended or in trouble with officials countless times, most infamously for his nose-breaking forearm tackle on Australian winger Paul Carozza during the second test of New Zealand's 1992 tour, and his eye-gouging of Otago fullback Greg Cooper during the 1992 national championship final.
He escaped punishment for the first offence but was banned from rugby for nine months, reduced to six on appeal, over the second incident.

The 37-year-old farmer, who played 78 matches for the All Blacks including 49 tests, expressed a general regret for his more ugly on-field moments, but blamed them on his tough upbringing in the sport.
"I grew up playing rugby in a fairly tough environment where front-row forwards were physical," he told Radio New Zealand.
"I was brought up that way. Front-row forwards were meant to be reasonably aggressive towards their game, and that's the way I played."
Greater media and television coverage of professional rugby matches has cleaned up the game, and violence which was once overlooked on the field is now strictly monitored and punished.
Loe appeared unconcerned that he might pass into history as one of the game's villains. Earlier this year he was named in a British list of the game's all-time dirtiest 10 players.
"Twenty years of top rugby, I'm quite proud of that," he said.
Loe rated his first game for the All Blacks, as a replacement against the French Barbarians in 1986, as his biggest rugby highlight, along with his test debut against Italy during the 1987 World Cup.
"When you're out there, especially for the All Blacks, you're doing your job and that is to represent New Zealand and make sure you win," he said.
"As far as the incidents go, of course you regret them and wish they hadn't happened, but you can't change history, you can only make it."
